evidence.title: Perception and challenges of artificial intelligence (AI) in Emergency Medicine: A multi-country study in Sub-Saharan Africa
evidence.venue: African journal of emergency medicine : Revue africaine de la medecine d'urgence
evidence.outcome: Institutions having a formal AI implementation strategy
evidence.effect: Only 12.0% of respondents indicated their institution had a formal AI implementation strategy.
evidence.quote: Only12.0 % indicated that their institution had a formal AI implementation strategy.
evidence.sample_unit: emergency medicine consultants and residents (survey responses)

commentary.bottom_line: Eleven sources endorse a system-wide AI strategy that uses a structured framework to prioritize use cases and assess resources, but no study has tested whether this practice reduces adoption of low-value or infeasible AI. The only supplied study is a survey showing that formal strategies were uncommon among the institutions sampled.

perspectives.view: No study compares organizations that use a structured prioritization framework with those that do not. One cross-sectional survey of 211 emergency clinicians found that 12.0% reported a formal institutional AI strategy. This study documents that strategies are often absent. It does not show that their absence leads to low-value adoption or that a framework prevents it. Endorsements rest on expert opinion.

The survey measured whether a strategy existed and did not measure errors, harms, or failed deployments. The supplied evidence therefore cannot tell us whether a structured framework catches unsafe or poorly suited tools before they reach patients. The link between planning and patient harm remains untested.

Several endorsing frameworks ask leaders to weigh personnel, lifecycle resources, and allocation across competing AI systems. No supplied study reports the staff time, cost, or governance capacity that such a framework requires, or whether it changes which tools a system buys. The 12.0% figure suggests many institutions would be building this capacity from the start.

The hazard survey drew respondents from 14 sub-Saharan African countries, which may reflect resource-limited settings, but it did not describe patient populations and was not conducted in U.S. Medicaid or safety-net systems. The HEAAL framework names resource and personnel assessment as equity components, yet no study tests whether applying it changes outcomes for underserved patients.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare health systems with and without a structured AI prioritization framework and that measure outcomes such as the share of deployed tools later retired, total spending on AI, staff effort, clinical or operational impact, and adverse events. Such studies should also report what it costs to run the framework and whether its use differs by organization size and resources.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tests the practice, so there is no evidence on its effect in Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The single hazard survey sampled emergency clinicians in sub-Saharan Africa and did not report patient characteristics. This suggests that safety-net systems, which may have the fewest resources for feasibility assessment, currently have no tested guidance on which framework to use or what it would require.
